# Versioning

How a campaign's work is held in version control: the repositories it works in, their
branches and worktrees, how a batch lands its work and how each part is promoted. Where
things sit in the tree is [`layout`](../layout/SKILL.md)'s.

## 1. Repositories

A translation campaign produces a Rust codebase, so its repository is one: a new
repository created for the campaign, with the Rust at its root and the C it translates
inside it.

| campaign | repository | the C, under `c/` |
|---|---|---|
| wrap | `<repo>-crustify` | a submodule of the source, pinned at the campaign's revision, which the campaign never changes |
| port | `<repo>-crustify` | a submodule of the campaign's fork of the source, `<repo>-fork`, on its `main` branch, which the modules' switches trim as they leave C |

`<repo>` is the source repository's name: a campaign on libgit2 is `libgit2-crustify`,
and a port's fork `libgit2-fork`. A wrap and a port campaign share the name, since wrapping a
codebase is a step towards replacing its implementation: a port continues a wrap campaign
in its repository. Both keep the C's history where it belongs, so that it can be read in the
submodule and an upstream release taken in by rebasing the fork's `main` onto it. The fork
mirrors the source's own `main` as `upstream/main`. The repositories are created under the
`crustify-rs` organization; the campaign's tree is [`layout`](../layout/SKILL.md)'s.

A library the target uses from outside its tree is wrapped in a wrap campaign of its own,
in `<source>-crustify`, named after the source it is built from, as
[`dependencies`](../../planning/dependencies/SKILL.md) describes.

An audit reviews an existing Rust crate in its own repository, and creates none.

## 2. Branches

| branch | name | checked out |
|---|---|---|
| shipping | `main` in the campaign's own repository; `crustify/main` in an audit, beside the reviewed crate's own branches | never while the campaign runs |
| working | `crustify/devel` | in the repository's base dir |
| planner run | `crustify/planner/run-<n>` | in the repository's base dir, while its run is live |
| module | `crustify/modules/<link-unit>/<module>`, or `crustify/foundational/<link-unit>/<module>` for a foundational module | in its worktree, while it integrates |
| wave | `crustify/waves/wave-<index>` | never |
| batch | `crustify/batches/wave-<index>/batch-<index>` | in its worktree |

The shipping branch holds what the user has approved to ship: it advances only with the
user's approval, by a fast-forward to the working branch, and each advance is tagged on it,
`ship-<n>` numbered from 1, or `crustify/ship-<n>` in an audit. The working branch is where the
campaign integrates its work: planner runs fork from it and are promoted back to it, and
the modules are integrated into it, as `scheduling` describes.

A module's branch holds one run of its waves: its waves fork from
it and are promoted back to it, and it is integrated into the working branch once they
have landed, as [Integration](#45-integration) describes. `<module>` is the module's
`name`, the path of its TU or header below the C root; a path is never a directory of
another, so no two module branches collide.

A wave's branch is the integration branch its batches land on, a review wave's as much as
a translation wave's. It is never checked out: a landing push to a checked-out branch
fails, and one to a missing branch silently creates it.

An audit has no link units or modules: its waves are review waves, laid out the same
way.

## 3. Worktrees

Each batch has its own worktree, its `c/` a worktree of the base checkout's submodule, at
`crustify/.worktrees/<module dir>/<batch id>`, named as
[`layout`](../layout/SKILL.md)'s Ids section names them, so that its name tells which
module it works on, and so does a module while it integrates, at
`crustify/.worktrees/<module dir>/integration`, beside its batches'. A
planner run has none: it runs in the repository's base dir, on its branch.

## 4. Landing

A batch lands its commits on the integration branch it was given, which is never checked
out. Before committing, the diff is checked to contain no unrelated work. A commit carries
no trailer but the co-author trailers of the campaign's [identity](#6-identity), and its
subject says what it does and which run made it. A batch's names its module's file and its
objective and ends with its run's id, as `refs.c: wrap 12 items (wave-3/batch-1/run-2)`,
and its body lists the items it translated by their anchors' paths, as
`fn::git_reference_lookup`, one per line; a review batch's two commits name what they file
and what they fix the same way, and a planner run's subject ends with its run's id. A
progress commit is `progress: wave-<index>`, and an integration's merge, in the campaign's
repository and on the fork's `main`, `integrate <module>`, the module written as
[`modules-schema`](../../artifacts/modules-schema/SKILL.md) writes it.

The landing operation is a local push of the batch's tip to the integration branch through
the repository's Git common directory, which accepts only a fast-forward. A direct ref
update is no substitute: its compare-and-swap form makes the update atomic, but does not
enforce that the new commit descends from the expected old commit.

### 4.1 The landing lock

An integration branch is landed on by one batch at a time, under its landing lock: an
exclusive `flock` on a file in the Git common directory, named after the branch with its
`refs/heads/` prefix dropped, so that every worktree of the repository sees the same lock:

```text
$(git rev-parse --git-common-dir)/crustify/landing/<integration branch>.lock
```

A batch whose validated work is committed on its own branch takes the lock and holds it
until its landing has succeeded:

1. it acquires the lock, waiting while another batch holds it;
2. it rebases only its own branch onto the current integration branch, once: nothing else
   lands while it holds the lock;
3. it resolves any conflict the rebase raises and runs again, on the rebased tree, the
   gates that could catch a regression of the integration, as
   [`testing-gates`](../../verification/testing/gates/SKILL.md)'s Regressions section describes, fixing what fails;
4. it pushes the fast-forward, which nothing can reject; and
5. it releases the lock.

A conflict or a failing gate is resolved under the lock rather than after releasing it, so
that the branch cannot move again in between and no batch rebases twice.

The waiter blocks in `flock` itself, so the kernel wakes it the moment the lock is released,
and nothing polls. Once it holds the lock, it hands the locked descriptor to a process of
its own, detached from the shell that started it and bound to the lifetime of the agent's
CLI: a `flock` lock belongs to the open file, so that process keeps it after the command
that took it exits, until that CLI ends, however it ends, and the kernel releases it. The
holder records itself beside the lock, in `<integration branch>.lock.holder`, as its own pid
and the CLI's. A waiter bounds each wait, to stay within the time a single command may run,
and waits again when it expires. For example, with `$CLI_PID` the agent CLI's pid, found by
walking up the shell's parent processes:
<!-- TODO: this procedure must run exactly so: it belongs in a script beside this skill,
documented by its `--help`, as `authoring` describes. -->

```bash
lock="$(git rev-parse --git-common-dir)/crustify/landing/<integration branch>.lock"
mkdir -p "$(dirname "$lock")"
# wait in the kernel, up to 10 minutes per command; then hand the lock to a detached holder
sh -c '
  exec 9>"$1"
  flock -w 600 9 || exit 1
  setsid sh -c "echo \"\$\$ $2\" > \"$1.holder\"; exec tail --pid=$2 -f /dev/null" 9>&9 &
' sh "$lock" "$CLI_PID"
# release, once the push has succeeded
holder=$(cut -d' ' -f1 "$lock.holder"); rm -f "$lock.holder"; kill "$holder"
```

The holder file is removed before the holder is ended, while the lock is still held, so
that a release never removes the next holder's record.

The lock has no timeout: the regression gates it covers vary in length. A holder that has
stopped making progress keeps it until its agent is ended. That releases it where the
agent ran in a CLI of its own. An agent that shared its CLI with others leaves its holder
running: the holder is then ended as a release ends it, by the pid its record names, the
record removed first. The batch is then run again, as any failed batch is.

### 4.2 Commits

Every landing is a fast-forward, so an integration branch is linear, and each batch's
commits are one unbroken run of it, ending at its branch's tip and starting after the wave
base or the tip of the batch that landed before it: the commits its branch reaches and
neither the wave base nor the wave's other landed batches reach, oldest first, which
become the batch's `commits` in `schedule.json`.

The integration branch is never reset, force-updated or moved backward, and nothing is
pushed to a remote. The worktree stays after landing, until it is purged as [Lifecycle](#5-lifecycle)
describes.
<!-- TODO: when the working and shipping branches, and a wrapper's, are pushed to their
remotes is not specified yet, though a wrapper's reuse and a Git-pinned dependency need
it. -->

### 4.3 Promotion

A wave that has landed every batch is promoted to the branch it forked from, the module's
branch or the working branch, by a fast-forward to its tip, with the same local push
through the Git common directory, which rejects anything but a fast-forward.

### 4.4 Progress

The progress recorded while waves run, in `schedule.json`, the dashboard's usage and
campaign cells, and the `status` of a module in `modules.json` that a wrap batch ahead of
its consumer freezes, is committed on the working branch whenever no module is integrating. No agent writes
`schedule.json`, and no module branch changes it.

### 4.5 Integration

A module's branch is integrated into the working branch once the
last wave of its run has been promoted to it. Other modules may have been integrated since
it forked, so the working branch is merged into it, in its worktree, rather than the
other way around: the module's commits keep their ids, which its batches' `commits`
record, and the working branch still moves only by fast-forward.

1. The working branch's tip is merged into the module's branch. The files every module
   adds to, the dashboard's rows, the raw bindings' allowlists, `src/lib.rs`'s module
   declarations and the safe crate's export features, conflict additively, and so does a
   module's file in which two runs homed different items ahead of their consumers, with
   the declarations of the modules on its path: each conflict
   keeps both sides, a file's items in one of each of its regions, and the generated bindings are regenerated from the merged input. Any other conflict is a defect of the integration, resolved without
   discarding either side. No merge is committed while its tree holds a conflict marker,
   here or wherever a branch takes another by merge, such as a wave's branch taking the
   working branch, so that every branch forked from it starts from a tree that builds.
2. The merge's tree passes the gates of
   [`testing-gates`](../../verification/testing/gates/SKILL.md)'s Regressions section, and in
   a port campaign, in the run that holds the last wave of the module's `wrap` and `port`
   items, the module's switch from C to Rust, which happens once, as
   [`porting-workflow`](../../workflows/porting-workflow/SKILL.md)'s Builds section describes:
   its export feature is deleted, and the C test cases none of its `unit_pub` tests carries
   over are listed before its C tests leave.
3. The working branch is fast-forwarded to the module's branch.

Modules integrate one at a time, and nothing else is committed on the working branch while
one does, so that its fast-forward cannot be rejected. A port's later-stage waves come after
their module's switch, are promoted to the working branch, and integrate nothing, as
the porting workflow's Later stages section describes.

## 5. Lifecycle

Each branch and worktree exists only while its part of the campaign needs it. Before a part starts, everything it is named for exists; once it is promoted, what
only it needed is purged.

### 5.1 Campaign

The working branch is created during setup, in the repository the campaign creates, with
the C under `c/` and `crustify/CRUSTIFY.md` in its first commit. The shipping branch is created at the same commit and stays there
until the user first approves shipping. Both last for the campaign.

The working branch is committed to only when nothing is being promoted or integrated to
it, so that every promotion and integration is a fast-forward: the progress recorded in
the meantime stays in the base checkout's working tree until then, as
[Progress](#44-progress) describes.

### 5.2 Planner runs

A planner run's branch is forked from the working branch's tip and checked out in the repository's base dir. Once the run has committed, the working
branch is checked out and fast-forwarded to it, and the next run forks from there.

### 5.3 Modules

A module's base is the working branch's commit that holds its scaffolded `.rs` file and
the settings it runs under, committed before its first wave.

A module's branch is forked from its base before its first wave,
once the waves of other modules that its waves depend on have been integrated. A module
whose waves the order splits, such as one that wraps a cut dependency ahead of its
consumer, or one whose wave waits for an item another module's run holds, as
[`scheduling`](../../planning/scheduling/SKILL.md)'s Wrap batches section describes, runs once per contiguous run of its waves, each run on a branch forked anew
from the working branch. In a port campaign, only the run that holds the last wave of the
module's `wrap` and `port` items switches it from C; an earlier run's integration merges
its Rust alone, the module still C. Once a run has been integrated, its branch and worktree
are purged; its end state is the working branch's commit its last run integrates into.

### 5.4 Waves

A wave's integration branch is forked from its module's branch's tip, or, for a port's
later-stage wave, which runs after its module's switch, from the working branch's tip,
before any of its batches launch, so that it exists before the first landing, as [Branches](#2-branches)
requires; that commit is the wave's base.
Once every batch has landed, the wave is promoted, as [Promotion](#43-promotion)
describes, and its branch purged.

A translation wave's review batches are batches of the wave itself, and it is promoted once
they have landed too. An audit's review waves fork as any wave does.

### 5.5 Batches

A batch's branch and worktree, forked from its wave branch's tip, are created before it
launches, with its run dir, as [`layout`](../layout/SKILL.md) describes. The gitignored state its tree needs and does
not build itself, such as shared analysis databases, is symlinked from the base checkout,
and its `c/` is a worktree of the base checkout's submodule at the commit the superproject
records, since no batch changes the C.
Once the batch has landed, its worktree is purged; its branch stays until its commits are
recorded in `schedule.json`, since they are derived from it, as
[Landing](#4-landing) describes. A batch that fails keeps its branch and worktree for
inspection; they are removed before it is run again, which forks them anew.

## 6. Identity

Every commit of a campaign, in its repository and its wrappers', is authored and committed
as Crustify, whose GitHub account is `crustify-ai` and whose git identity is
`crustify <crustify@berkeley.edu>`, whatever the repository's git configuration says,
unless the settings' `identity` answer names another: an author and any co-authors, each
as `Name <email>`. The author named there then authors and commits every commit, and each
message ends with one `Co-Authored-By:` trailer per co-author and no other, none that an
agent's host suggests included.

The identity is passed explicitly, as configuration on the command line, to every command
that writes a commit, a rebase, a merge and a cherry-pick as much as a commit, since the
host may have no git identity of its own.

once the waves of other modules that its waves depend on have been integrated. A module
whose waves the order splits, such as one that wraps a cut dependency ahead of its
consumer, or one whose wave waits for an item another module's run holds, as
[`scheduling`](../../planning/scheduling/SKILL.md)'s Wrap batches section describes, runs once per contiguous run of its waves, each run on a branch forked anew
from the working branch. In a port campaign, only the run that holds the last wave of the
module's `wrap` and `port` items switches it from C; an earlier run's integration merges
its Rust alone, the module still C. Once a run has been integrated, its branch and worktree
are purged; its end state is the working branch's commit its last run integrates into.

### 5.4 Waves

A wave's integration branch is forked from its module's branch's tip, or, for a port's
later-stage wave, which runs after its module's switch, from the working branch's tip,
before any of its batches launch, so that it exists before the first landing, as [Branches](#2-branches)
requires; that commit is the wave's base.

describes, and its branch purged.

A translation wave's review batches are batches of the wave itself, and it is promoted once
they have landed too. An audit's review waves fork as any wave does.

### 5.5 Batches

A batch's branch and worktree, forked from its wave branch's tip, are created before it
launches, with its run dir, as [`layout`](../layout/SKILL.md) describes. The gitignored state its tree needs and does
not build itself, such as shared analysis databases, is symlinked from the base checkout,

records, since no batch changes the C.

recorded in `schedule.json`, since they are derived from it, as
[Landing](#4-landing) describes. A batch that fails keeps its branch and worktree for
inspection; they are removed before it is run again, which forks them anew.

## 6. Identity

as `Name <email>`. The author named there then authors and commits every commit, and each
message ends with one `Co-Authored-By:` trailer per co-author and no other, none that an
agent's host suggests included.

The identity is passed explicitly, as configuration on the command line, to every command
that writes a commit, a rebase, a merge and a cherry-pick as much as a commit, since the
host may have no git identity of its own.

# Campaign layout

Where a campaign's files sit: the repository's tree, its artifact dirs, Crustify's home
and the campaign's scratch and reviews dirs. The repositories, branches and worktrees
that hold them are [`versioning`](../versioning/SKILL.md)'s.

A repository holds one campaign, and its work is cumulative: a later run resumes it and
skips what it already completed. Its artifact and reviews dirs are grouped by module, and
named from a batch's coordinates in `crustify/artifacts/schedule.json`, its module, wave
index and batch index, and a run's attempt. Nothing records a path; each name below is
spelled from those coordinates.

## 1. Tree

A translation campaign's repository, as [`versioning`](../versioning/SKILL.md)'s Repositories
section names it, is laid out as:

```text
<repository>/
├── Cargo.toml          the safe crate, and the workspace
├── src/                the safe crate's modules, as the conventions lay them out
├── tests/              the safe crate's integration test suites
├── sys/                the raw bindings' generator input and generated bindings, one dir per link unit
├── c/                  the C codebase, the C root, which the safe crate bundles
└── crustify/           the campaign: its settings, artifacts and analysis state
```

The wrappers of the libraries it uses from outside its tree are repositories of their
own, cloned beside it as `../<source>-crustify`, as [`dependencies`](../../planning/dependencies/SKILL.md)
describes.

Every path into the C that the plan records, in `modules.json`, `schedule.json`, the
tools' configurations and tables and a batch item's `defined_in`, is relative to the C
root, `c/`, so that the plan reads as the C codebase lays itself out. Every other path is
relative to the repository's root.

## 2. Ids

A batch's id is the part of its branch name after `crustify/batches/`:
`wave-<index>/batch-<index>`. It is permanent, since a started wave's index is never
reused or renumbered (see `schedule-schema`), and its entry in `schedule.json` gives the batch's link
unit, module, kind and worklist. A run's id is its batch's id followed by its attempt,
numbered from 1 in the order the batch's runs launch: `wave-3/batch-1/run-2`. A planner
run's is `planner/run-<n>`, numbered among the planner runs, which also names its branch.

A module's dir is its branch's name after `crustify/`: `modules/<link-unit>/<module>`, or
`foundational/<link-unit>/<module>` for a foundational module. A wave that belongs to no
module, such as an audit's, has `waves` in its place.

## 3. Artifact dirs

The campaign's artifacts sit under `crustify/artifacts/`, with one dir per agent run:

```text
crustify/artifacts/                             the campaign
├── build.json                                  the prebuilt variants of the target
├── modules.json                                the module decomposition
├── dependencies.json                           the out-of-tree libraries the target uses
├── schedule.json                               the waves and batches, and their progress
├── dashboard.md                                the campaign dashboard; audit-dashboard.md for an audit
├── planner/run-<n>/                            a planner run
├── evolution/<slug>/review-<n>/                a review of a change to Crustify or a tool
└── <module dir>/wave-<index>/                  a wave's dir: its own records, such as its scans
    └── batch-<index>/run-<n>/                  a run of a batch, a binder's, a translator's or a reviewer's
        ├── task.json                           its input, with the batch and run fields, and its session id
        ├── task.md                             its task message
        └── …                                   the records its run keeps, as the tool skills name them
```

A batch that is run again gets a new run dir, and every attempt keeps its records. A run's
`task.json` names its batch too. The run dir holds
what the campaign keeps of the run: its input, with the backend, billing, model proxy and
arguments it ran under and the session it became, and the artifacts its agent produced.
Its transcript and pricing record are in crustify's home.

The settings each module or wave ran under are not copied anywhere: they are
`crustify/CRUSTIFY.md` as committed at its base, in the working branch's history.

## 4. Lifecycle

A run's dir, with its `task.json`, is created before its agent launches, and kept: every
attempt keeps its records. The campaign's artifact dir is created during setup, with the
working branch.

## 5. Crustify's home

Crustify keeps what belongs to its user rather than to a campaign in its home,
`$CRUSTIFY_HOME` or `~/.crustify`:

```text
~/.crustify/
├── providers/<backend>/              a CLI's config home under API-key billing
├── sessions/<session id>/
│   └── usage.session.json            how a session was priced: its backend, model proxy and rate snapshot
├── rates/<timestamp>.json            the rates `crustify-usage` fetched, kept whenever they changed
└── transcripts/<session id>.jsonl    the agents' transcripts, copied from the CLIs' homes
```

A session's directory is named by its CLI's session id, which its run's `task.json`
records, or, for an agent its host runs inside another session, by the agent's id.

## 6. Scratch

`crustify/tmp/` is gitignored and holds anything residual that is no artifact: downloads,
scratch builds and experiments, intermediate outputs. Residual files go nowhere else in the
repository. An agent's scratch is its own: its worktree's `crustify/tmp/`, never a
directory the host hands every agent of a session, such as a scratchpad its subagents
share, where another agent's run can overwrite it.

## 7. Reviews

A review batch's findings sit under its reviews dir, `crustify/reviews/<module dir>/<batch id>/`,
such as `crustify/reviews/modules/libgit2/src/libgit2/refs.c/wave-3/batch-1/`, in the repository the review lands in, and a planner
run's plan corrections under `crustify/reviews/planner/`, as
[`reviewing`](../../verification/reviewing/SKILL.md)'s Reports and Plan corrections sections
lay them out.

## 8. Evolution

The campaign's lessons sit in `crustify/LESSONS.md`, and its proposals for Crustify and its
tools under `crustify/evolution/<slug>/`, as [`evolution`](../../crustify/evolution/SKILL.md)
describes.

# Accounting

What a campaign records about its own work: the dashboard, the runs' records and
transcripts its figures come from, and how cost and time are derived from them.

## 1. The dashboard

The dashboard, `crustify/artifacts/dashboard.md` unless the settings name another, is the
campaign's record of what each planner run, batch, wave and module did and cost. It is
filled from `templates/translate/dashboard.template.md`, an audit's from
`templates/audit/dashboard.template.md`, and keeps the template's format exactly.
When an adopted Crustify change adds a table or a column to the template, it is
added to the dashboard on the working branch before the next batch launches: a batch
fills the rows of the tables in place, and never adds one.

It is tracked in the campaign's tree, so every agent's worktree holds a copy, and it is
filled as the work lands rather than at the end. Each figure is measured once, where it is
produced: no suite or scan is rerun only to record one.

## 2. Cells

The dashboard's cells fall into three kinds, by when their figures can be known.

### 2.1 Landing cells

The cells measured on the tree a landing commits:

- for a batch, under the route its items' `kind` selects, as
  [`task-schema`](../../artifacts/task-schema/SKILL.md)'s Routes section gives it: its rows
  in that route's `Batches`, tests, `Batches: safety audit` and `Batches: API stability` tables, and for a review batch in
  `Batches — review: PoC + reports`, each placed in module, wave and batch order under
  its `pass`, and for a module pass, which spans both routes, in `Module passes`; those
  tables' `Σ` rows; and the `Coverage stats` table and the Overview's LoC
  line;
- for a planner run, its row in `Planning`, but for its usage cells.

They are filled in the landing's last commit, and measured against the integration branch
tip it was rebased onto: coverage as [`testing-builds`](../../verification/testing/builds/SKILL.md)'s Coverage section measures
it, the safety audit columns as the changes in the dashboard's Safety audit metrics, and
the API stability columns as the changes to the API of the landing's items are classified. A
rebase that conflicts in the dashboard keeps every row both sides added, and the landing's
cells, `Σ` rows included, are measured again where the gates its rebase reruns cover them;
the others stand as measured on the batch's base.

An integration merge, and any merge of one branch into another, keeps every row both
sides added, and settles the rest so: an additive `Σ` cell is the sum over the merged
rows, ours plus theirs less the merge base's, and so are the Overview's `Rust LoC`
figures; a usage `Σ` cell, its per-unit cells included, sums only the rows that carry
usage, so that it is filled again with theirs; a coverage `Σ` cell, and the Overview's
`C LoC`, are the later landing's; and `Coverage stats` takes the merged suites' counts,
with the later landing's percentages until a gate measures the merged tree, which the
merge commit's message says. A table or section the template holds once is kept once,
with the rows of every copy, whether or not the merge conflicts there, and the merged
dashboard is checked for repeated headings before it is committed.

### 2.2 Usage cells

The cells known only once an agent has ended, from its usage: its cost, tokens and wall,
the per-unit costs derived from them, and their `Σ` cells. A batch's are filled on the
working branch once its row is there, once its module is integrated, as
[`versioning`](../versioning/SKILL.md) describes, or, for a port's later-stage batch, which
runs after its module's switch, once its wave is promoted. A planner run's are filled once the run is
promoted. A batch run more than once costs the sum of its runs.

### 2.3 Campaign cells

The cells that span agents: the `Module stats` table, the Overview's branch line and
test baseline, and the `Settings` lines. A module's row and the branch line are filled
when the module is integrated, and a port's module row again as each of its later-stage
waves is promoted, the baseline once it is recorded, and the `Settings` lines,
with a Notes entry, whenever a settings change is applied.

### 2.4 Side campaign cells

A side campaign keeps its own dashboard, in its own repository, and its figures are
measured there. The parent's `Side campaigns` table copies them, one row per wrapper, as
they stand at the commit the parent pins, and the `side campaigns` row of `Module stats`
sums the rows, so that the parent's `Σ campaign` covers what its side campaigns cost. A
wrapper's row is filled each time the parent's pin moves, and its `shipped at` cell when
the wrapper ships the commit the parent pins. A side campaign that serves several parents
appears in each, with the figures as of each one's pin.

An audit's dashboard follows the same kinds over its own tables.

## 3. Records

Every run's `task.json` records how its agent ran: its backend, billing, model proxy and
the arguments its CLI was given, and, once it starts, its `session_id`, which ties the run
to its session. The session's transcript, which its CLI keeps by session id, is the
agent's full log and the source of its accounting. An agent spawned as a subagent of
another session has no session of its own: its session id is `agent-<agent id>`, the
name its host gives its transcript, under the spawning session's `subagents/`.

A transcript is copied into crustify's home, as `transcripts/<session id>.jsonl`, as soon
as its agent ends, because the CLIs move and prune their own files. Its usage is derived
from the copy, as [`usage`](../usage/SKILL.md) describes, with the backend and model proxy its
`task.json` names.

An evolution review is a run like any other: its `task.json` sits in its artifact dir, and
its transcript is collected and priced the same way, its cost counted with the sessions that
orchestrate the campaign and recorded, with its tokens and wall time, in its proposal's
Review section, so that what each review bought can be weighed against its cost.

The sessions that orchestrate the campaign are collected the same way: at the start of each session, the
transcripts of the sessions before it. A resumed session keeps its id while its transcript
grows: its transcript is copied again after each run, replacing the earlier copy. The
records, transcripts and rates stay in crustify's home.

## 4. Cost and time

A run's cost and tokens are its usage's `total.cost_usd` and `total.tokens`, as
[`usage`](../usage/SKILL.md) derives them from its transcript. The computed cost is used, never a provider-reported
dollar total; under subscription billing it is the API-equivalent cost.

An agent's wall time is its usage's interval. A wave's runs from its first batch's
launch through its final review and regression gates, a review wave's in an audit through
its landing, and a module's from its first launch through its final gate.

# Evolution

How a campaign changes the harness that runs it, Crustify's skills, agents, templates and
providers, its tools and the tools it lacks, and how its agents propose changes to the
campaign's artifacts that other roles own. A campaign exposes what the harness gets
wrong, what it constrains needlessly and what it repeats by hand; evolution turns that
evidence into changes, under the autonomy the settings' `evolution` answer grants, and
this guidance itself among them. Where a change goes within Crustify is
[`authoring`](../authoring/SKILL.md)'s.

## 1. Goals

Every change is judged against Crustify's goals, [`GOALS.md`](../../../GOALS.md), read in
full before the first proposal: a change serves one of them, or it is not made. The goals
are evolved too, when the evidence questions them, as `GOALS.md` describes.

A change to a tool is judged against that tool's own goals and non-goals too, the document
its tool skill names, read in full before the first change to the tool: they keep what the
tool is from drifting, such as an analysis that stays syntactic and does no data-flow
analysis. A change that departs from one of them is proposed, not made, and says so. A
tool with no such document has every change that alters what it is, rather than fixing or
extending what it does, proposed, not made.
<!-- TODO: ffimap has no goals document yet. -->

## 2. Signals

Evolution starts from evidence a campaign produces, never from taste:

| signal | what it suggests |
|---|---|
| a tool that crashes, or reports what the source contradicts | a defect in the tool |
| skills that contradict each other, or an agent prompt that leads its agent wrong | a defect in the spec |
| a rule an agent works around, or that forces a worse result than its omission would | an overconstraining rule, loosened or removed |
| review findings that recur across batches, in one objective or category | a rule the how-to skills lack |
| failed or rerun batches, and plan corrections | a defect in planning, scheduling or packing |
| the user's corrections | a rule, or a lesson of the campaign |
| cost or time outliers, in the dashboard | waste in batch sizing, gates or tooling |
| one representation hand-written in several places, or a TODO met again and again | a primitive or tool feature that is missing |
| one procedure repeated by hand: the same script written again, the same queries run in sequence | a tool, or a subcommand of one |
| a signal evolution missed, or a proposal that proved wrong | a defect in this guidance |
| a goal no decision cites, two that keep conflicting the same way, or a well-founded change no goal serves | a change to the goals |

A proposal needs one of these, with its evidence: a defect, a failure, a recurring
finding, a workaround or a measured waste. Fewer, well-founded proposals serve better than
many small ones: a change made for style alone, or for completeness, or to have proposed
something, is not made.

## 3. Destinations

Each signal goes to one destination:

- **the campaign alone**: what a setting or a task message settles, which changes nothing
  of Crustify;
- **a lesson**: a rule that holds for this target alone, recorded in the campaign's
  [`LESSONS.md`](#5-lessons);
- **the spec**: a skill, an agent, a template or a provider, where `authoring` places it;
- **a tool**: its code, its documentation or its tests, or a new tool; or
- **a campaign artifact**: the plan, the dependencies, the schedule or the dashboard, where
  the evidence shows one wrong or improvable and another role owns it. Its owner applies
  the proposal or declines it, a plan's at the next planner run.

A rule an agent cannot follow because its host refuses it, a write or a tool call
blocked, or a launch mode that withholds what the role needs, is a defect of that host's
provider, not of the rule: the provider prevents it with whatever its host offers, its
agents' definitions, the settings and permissions it installs, its hooks, the mode it
launches runs in, or the host's memory, and the spec is not bent around one host. Until
the provider's change lands, a run that meets the refusal neither works around it nor drops
what it could not do: it hands that to the assistant, in its final message, and the
assistant carries it out.

The test between a lesson and the spec is generality: a rule that can only be stated in
the target's own names is a lesson, and one the spec takes is stated without them, as it
would hold for any C codebase.

## 4. Proposals

A proposal is filed in the campaign's repository under `crustify/evolution/<slug>/`, as
its `PROPOSAL.md`: the signal and its evidence, with the runs, findings and commits it
cites; its destination; the change, or the patch; how it was validated; its review's
verdict; and its status, `open`, `landed`, with the commit it landed as, or `declined`,
with why. A lesson is not
filed as a proposal: `LESSONS.md` records it.

A defect in a tool found while reviewing is such a proposal, not a finding on the reviewed
code, and is filed with its reproducer.

## 5. Lessons

The campaign's lessons sit in `crustify/LESSONS.md`, read by every run of the campaign
before its first step. Each is one rule, with the evidence it rests on and its scope, the
modules, items or stages it holds for. A lesson a second campaign records again is
generalized into the spec, by a proposal citing both.

## 6. Changes

A campaign evolves each component, Crustify or a tool, on a working branch of its own in
that component's repository, `<campaign-id>/devel`, the campaign id being the name of the
campaign's repository. It is forked from the component's `devel` when the campaign first
needs it, and the campaign's runs read and run the component from its checkout, so that a
campaign runs on what it has changed and no other campaign does.

A change is made on a branch named `<campaign-id>/evolution/<slug>`, forked from that
working branch, in a worktree beside the repository that lives only while the change is
made. A branch holds one concern. Once the change lands on the working branch, by a
fast-forward, the worktree is purged and the branch deleted. Its commits take the identity
[`versioning`](../../operations/versioning/SKILL.md)'s Identity section gives the
campaign's.

- A change to the spec follows `authoring`: written once, in the place its kind belongs,
  as generally as the evidence allows.
- A change to what a tool does comes with a regression test: the reproducer of a defect
  becomes one, and a new behaviour gets one that fails without it. A change to its
  documentation alone adds none, unless the defect it fixes has a reproducer, which becomes
  a test or a doctest. A packaging defect's reproducer becomes a test too, run
  against a build installed as a dependent installs it. The tool's whole suite passes, its
  opt-in tests included wherever the change touches what they cover.
- A new tool is drafted and tested where it serves a repeated procedure, preferably as a
  subcommand of an existing tool within that tool's goals, or as a script in the skill
  that describes its use, as `authoring` places one; a tool of its own repository is
  merged upstream only with the user's approval.

A fix that unblocks the campaign, or that would prevent a defect in later campaigns, is
landed on the working branch as soon as it is reviewed, rather than batched.

## 7. Validation

A tool's change is validated by its tests, the regression test it adds among them.

A spec change that a failure prompted is validated by running again what failed, the item,
the batch or the stage, under the change: a lightweight run, without the tests or gates
the failure does not need to show. The proposal records what the run produced before and
after, and a change whose rerun still fails does not land. A spec change no failure
prompted, such as a rule loosened or a waste removed, is validated the same way where its
effect is in doubt, on the item its evidence came from.

A rerun shows that a change answers the case that exposed it, not that it holds: that is
watched in the campaigns after it lands, as [Record](#11-record) describes.

## 8. Review

Every change is reviewed before it lands, on its evolution branch, by a run other than the
one that made it. The review reads the proposal, the change and its validation, and checks
that:

- the proposal's evidence shows the signal, and the change answers it;
- the change serves a goal, and a tool's stays within the tool's own goals;
- it is placed and written as [`authoring`](../authoring/SKILL.md) describes, and states
  no rule in the target's names;
- its validation was run, and shows what the proposal says;
- its entry of [Record](#11-record), which the change or its proposal drafts, names a
  recurrence signal a campaign would observe, and `test` only where its test checks all of
  it; and
- whether it weakens a check, which the verdict marks.

A review runs under the campaign's working branch of the component, never under the change
it reviews, and reads the change from its branch. Its task pins the commit it reviews, and
only that commit lands, by a fast-forward of the working branch: a commit added after the
verdict, or one a rebase or cherry-pick makes, is reviewed again. Its checks are this section's and its
role's; the task message of the run that asks for it adds to them, and never relaxes them.
A review reads as deeply as the change reaches: a change to documentation alone is read; a
tool's code, a check, a soundness fix and every rule of the spec are reviewed with their
validation run again.

The verdict is recorded in the proposal's Review section, approved or rejected, with its
reasons; a rejection leaves the proposal open for another change or for the user.

What only records what was decided, a status of [Record](#11-record) a check changes or a
proposal's status, verdict and review, changes no rule and is not reviewed; an entry is
reviewed with its change.

A change that weakens a check, a gate, a test, a lint, a review objective, a tool's
detection or a rule of this skill, is marked so in the verdict and in its entry of the
record, since a run that can loosen what judges it passes by loosening it: the user reads
each such change on its own before `devel` takes it, as [Autonomy](#9-autonomy) describes.

## 9. Autonomy

The settings' `evolution` answer sets how far a campaign evolves the harness:

| answer | what lands on the campaign's working branches |
|---|---|
| `off` | nothing: no proposal, no lesson |
| `propose` | nothing but the record's statuses: proposals and lessons are filed, and no rule changes |
| `repair` | each fix of a defect |
| `evolve` | also each improvement and discovery |

A change lands on its component's working branch as soon as its review approves it,
without the user's approval: the working branch is the campaign's own, and nothing else
runs on it. `GOALS.md` is the exception: a change to it is proposed, never made, since it
is what every other change is judged against.

A component's `devel` is the user's gate. It takes a campaign's working branch only with
the user's approval, asked for at each module's end and at the campaign's end, with the
record's entries since the last advance, those the review marked as weakening a check
first. Where `devel` has moved meanwhile, the working branch takes it by merge before it
is offered. What the user declines is reverted on the working branch or stays there, as
they say, and is recorded so; where it weakened a check, what landed under it is reviewed
again, by review batches with `revisit`, as [Adoption](#10-adoption) schedules them for a
soundness fix. Merging a component's `devel` into its `main`, and merging a
new tool upstream, need the user's approval too.

A run that a defect blocks does not work around it. Where the answer lets fixes land, it
makes the fix on its evolution branch; under `propose` it files the proposal, with its
reproducer, and the user is asked at once whether the fix is to be made; and it ends,
reporting which. The fix is reviewed and lands, and the run is run again, as a failed
batch is.

## 10. Adoption

Every run's `task.json` records the revisions of Crustify and the tools it launched
under, as [`task-schema`](../../artifacts/task-schema/SKILL.md)'s Run fields section
describes. A change that lands on a working branch takes effect as it lands: the runs launched
after it record its revision, and a run under way when it lands, which its recorded
revisions and its landing's date tell, may have followed either. What landed before it
under the old rules stays, unless the change fixes a soundness
defect: then the landings it affects are reviewed again, by a review batch with
`revisit`.

At each module's end, the campaign's evolution is consolidated: recurring lessons are
proposed for the spec, open proposals are landed as the autonomy allows, the working
branches are offered to the user for `devel`, the revisit batches a soundness fix or a declined weakening calls for are scheduled, and the watched changes
of the record are checked against the module, as an audit checks them at its end.

## 11. Record

Every change that lands is recorded in Crustify's own repository, in
[`EVOLUTION.md`](../../../EVOLUTION.md), whatever component it changed, so that a later
campaign can tell whether it held. An entry gives the campaign and proposal the change
came from, the component and commit it landed as, the signal it answered, its recurrence
signal and its status, with a change that weakens a check marked so in its status. A change
no proposal filed names its campaign and `no proposal` in its place, with where it came
from. The entry is drafted with its change, in the change itself for a
change to Crustify and in its proposal for a change to a tool, so that the review reads it,
and is committed on Crustify's working branch of the campaign as the change lands. The record holds every
change landed since it began, on 2026-11-12; what landed before is not recorded.

The recurrence signal is what a campaign would observe if the issue were back, in what a
campaign produces anyway: a review finding of a category, a run that fails for a cause, a
tool's error, a correction the user repeats. A change whose regression test checks all of
it has `test` in its place and is not watched. One with no signal a campaign could observe
has `none`, with why, and is not watched either.

A watched change is checked at each module's end, and at an audit's end, in every campaign,
against that module's or audit's findings, failed runs, proposals and corrections. It is:

- `watched` from its landing;
- `recurred` once its signal is met again, with the evidence, which opens a proposal that
  cites the entry: the change was wrong or partial, or the validation and review that
  passed it were; and
- `confirmed` once a campaign other than the one it came from has ended, having exercised
  it, without the signal.

The record is committed on Crustify's working branch of the campaign, each entry with its
change and each check at its module's end, and reaches `devel` with it. Rows are appended
in landing order and statuses edited in place, so that a merge of two campaigns' working
branches keeps both campaigns' rows, ordered by their landing.
Under `propose`, where no rule changes, the check still runs and its statuses are
committed all the same, since a record commit changes no rule, and they are put to the user
with the campaign's proposals. Under `off`, it does not run.

## 12. Evolving evolution

Evolution evolves from its own record, as everything else does from a campaign's. At a
campaign's end the record and the campaign's proposals are read for what repeats: changes
that recurred; changes the review rejected or the user declined, by cause; signals a run
met that no proposal answered; how long a blocking defect held its run; and what the
reviews bought for what they cost: per change, the findings each round made that held, those
its author's own validation had already caught, the rounds it took and their cost. How deep
a review reads, and how many rounds a kind of change gets, follow from that evidence, not
from a fixed rule. Each is a
signal of this guidance, as [Signals](#2-signals) lists them, and its proposal is on this
skill, on the agents' evolution rules or on what the review checks.

Such a proposal is validated and reviewed as any other, and is marked as one that changes
what checks the rest, so that the user reads it on its own before `devel` takes it, as
[Autonomy](#9-autonomy) describes.

signal and its status, with a change that weakens a check marked so in its status. A change
no proposal filed names its campaign and `no proposal` in its place, with where it came
from. The entry is drafted with its change, in the change itself for a
change to Crustify and in its proposal for a change to a tool, so that the review reads it,
and is committed on Crustify's working branch of the campaign as the change lands. The record holds every
change landed since it began, on 2026-11-12; what landed before is not recorded.

The recurrence signal is what a campaign would observe if the issue were back, in what a
campaign produces anyway: a review finding of a category, a run that fails for a cause, a
tool's error, a correction the user repeats. A change whose regression test checks all of
it has `test` in its place and is not watched. One with no signal a campaign could observe
has `none`, with why, and is not watched either.

A watched change is checked at each module's end, and at an audit's end, in every campaign,
against that module's or audit's findings, failed runs, proposals and corrections. It is:

- `watched` from its landing;
- `recurred` once its signal is met again, with the evidence, which opens a proposal that
  cites the entry: the change was wrong or partial, or the validation and review that
  passed it were; and
- `confirmed` once a campaign other than the one it came from has ended, having exercised
  it, without the signal.

The record is committed on Crustify's working branch of the campaign, each entry with its
change and each check at its module's end, and reaches `devel` with it. Rows are appended
in landing order and statuses edited in place, so that a merge of two campaigns' working
branches keeps both campaigns' rows, ordered by their landing.
Under `propose`, where no rule changes, the check still runs and its statuses are
committed all the same, since a record commit changes no rule, and they are put to the user
with the campaign's proposals. Under `off`, it does not run.

## 12. Evolving evolution

Evolution evolves from its own record, as everything else does from a campaign's. At a
campaign's end the record and the campaign's proposals are read for what repeats: changes
that recurred; changes the review rejected or the user declined, by cause; signals a run
met that no proposal answered; how long a blocking defect held its run; and what the
reviews bought for what they cost: per change, the findings each round made that held, those
its author's own validation had already caught, the rounds it took and their cost. How deep
a review reads, and how many rounds a kind of change gets, follow from that evidence, not
from a fixed rule. Each is a
signal of this guidance, as [Signals](#2-signals) lists them, and its proposal is on this
skill, on the agents' evolution rules or on what the review checks.

Such a proposal is validated and reviewed as any other, and is marked as one that changes
what checks the rest, so that the user reads it on its own before `devel` takes it, as
[Autonomy](#9-autonomy) describes.

---
name: ffimap
description: "Deterministic counts and sites of a Rust crate's unsafe and FFI surface. Read before a batch lands (its safe-boundary scan and safety-audit cells), before planning an audit's worksets, and when reviewing for unsafety, contracts or UB."
---

# ffimap

ffimap maps a Rust crate's FFI and unsafe surface deterministically: a rustc driver over
HIR and typeck counts unsafe blocks and fns, raw and void pointers by position and
visibility, FFI calls and wrapper use. No model is involved, so two runs over one tree
agree exactly. Its `--help` lists its flags, and its `docs/schema.md`, read in full before
its first scan, its counters and how a report combines them.

It counts what the build compiles of the safe crate itself, and prints one JSON document:

```bash
ffimap <workdir> > <file>.json
```

Every scan names the crate's seams, the functions that hand a value between its wrapper and
its raw form, so that each counter's `of_which.seam` share tells that plumbing apart from
the pointer management a consumer of the safe API faces: ffibox's handle seams `as_ptr`,
`as_mut_ptr`, `as_void_ptr`, `from_ptr` and `from_void_ptr`, the ownership hand-offs
`from_raw_parts`, `into_raw_parts`, `into_raw`, `from_c`, `into_c` and `as_c_ptr`, the adoption of a raw C
value, `from_raw`, and the view of a C object as another, `as_object`. A crate built on
ffibox is scanned with `--ffibox`, and its `-sys` crates are named with `--sys-crates`:

```bash
ffimap <workdir> --ffibox --sys-crates <the -sys crates> --regions ffi_import,ffi_export \
    --seams as_ptr,as_mut_ptr,as_void_ptr,from_ptr,from_void_ptr,from_raw_parts,into_raw_parts,into_raw,from_c,into_c,as_c_ptr,from_raw,as_object \
    > <file>.json
```

In a port campaign, a scan names with `--features` the export feature of every module not
yet switched, as the [conventions](../../rust/conventions/SKILL.md)' Export features section
names them, so that the `ffi_export` gateways compiled under them are counted. Every scan
names the module's unsafe regions, as the conventions' Unsafe regions section names them,
with `--regions`.

Two scans are compared only when they name the same seams, regions and features.

Its counters form one tree, each named by its dotted path into the scan's `counts`, as
ffimap's `docs/schema.md` describes; a metric is a counter, or a combination of counters
that schema allows: a partition's leaves summed, a share read against the record it cuts,
or subtracted from it. `--sites <counter> ...` also lists where each named counter's
increments are, and takes leaves only, such as `fn.unsafe.pub`; the workspace is named
before it. The counters that recur:

- `fn.unsafe.pub`, the public `unsafe fn`s, the crate's public unsafe surface, of which
  `fn.unsafe.of_which.other.pub` are those neither a trait nor a seam required; and
  `raw_ptr.fn_sig_arg.unsafe.pub` and `raw_ptr.fn_sig_ret.unsafe.pub`, the raw pointers in
  their signatures;
- `raw_ptr.field.pub`, `raw_ptr.fn_sig_arg.safe.pub` and `raw_ptr.fn_sig_ret.safe.pub`, the
  raw pointers in public fields and in the signatures of public safe fns, together
  `raw_ptr.total.safe.pub`, the raw pointers on the safe public interface; and their
  `of_which.void` shares, the type-erased ones among them;
- `ty.ffibox.wrapper.as.borrowed.std.{pub,priv}`, the references to a cell, less their
  `of_which.self_in_ref_accessor` and `of_which.self_in_trait_impl` shares, the positions
  ffibox sanctions: references to C memory where a handle belongs, which assert `noalias`,
  `readonly` or validity over memory C may write; `ty.ffibox.sys.as.borrowed.std`, the same
  of the raw C structs; and `raw_ptr.casted_to.std.{borrow,slice,string}`, the borrows,
  slices and strings formed from a raw pointer, over bytes C must neither free nor change
  while they live;
- `ty.impl_trait.of_which.std.send.{pub,priv}` and `ty.impl_trait.of_which.std.sync.{pub,priv}`,
  each an unchecked assertion that a value may move to or be shared with another thread;
- `raw_ptr.deref.wr` and `raw_ptr.deref.rd`, raw-pointer writes and reads, each a pointer
  the implementer vouches is non-null, aligned, live, initialized and unaliased by a live
  reference; and
- `ty.storing_raw_ptr.of_which.impl_drop.{pub,priv}` and
  `ty.storing_raw_ptr.of_which.impl_clone.{pub,priv}`, the types that hold a raw pointer and
  tear it down or copy it by hand, and `ty.storing_raw_ptr.of_which.none.{pub,priv}`, those
  that declare nothing about it. Each of these five also has a `.total`, the sum of its two
  leaves, which is no leaf for `--sites`.

ffimap is neither complete nor sound: its sites are where review starts, not all it
covers. It does not count the lifetimes formed inside `unsafe` blocks, such as a reference
or lifetime-annotated handle made from a raw pointer by `&*p`, `from_ptr`, `from_raw` or
`from_raw_parts`, or changed by a `transmute`: those are found in the source.

What follows is how ffimap serves each stage: each section names the skill and section it
adds to, and states only what ffimap adds there.

## Binding and porting

### Binding › Safe boundary

Before a batch lands, a scan with `--sites fn.unsafe.pub raw_ptr.field.pub
raw_ptr.fn_sig_arg.safe.pub raw_ptr.fn_sig_ret.safe.pub` lists the public
`unsafe fn`s and the raw pointers on the safe public interface, and each of those sites
that belongs to the batch's changeset and that a safe variant could replace is fixed.
Its `--sites` also name the unsafe code outside both regions,
`code.unsafe_block.of_which.outside_regions`, another crate's macro expansions included,
which the `unsafe_code` lint misses, and `fn.unsafe.of_which.outside_regions.pub` and
`.priv`: outside the raw bindings, each of those sites in the batch's changeset is moved
into its region.

## Accounting

### Accounting › Landing cells

A batch's row in the dashboard's `Batches: safety audit` table is the change in each of
the Safety audit's metrics, from a scan of the tip its landing rebased onto to a scan of
the tree it lands.

### Accounting › API stability

`ffimap api` measures a safe crate's consumer-facing API per C item, from rustdoc JSON, as
its `docs/api.md` describes, read in full before its first use. A C item is the
`<kind>::<path>` of a `Wraps` or `Replaces` anchor, its surface every stand-in the anchor
names and the handles and owners tied to it, each judged by the contract
[`binding-types`](../../rust/binding/types/SKILL.md)' Safe layout section gives a consumer:
the methods every form offers, its reborrows and dereferences, and the traits a consumer
can use, never a form's raw access or seams. A batch generates the safe crate's rustdoc
JSON on the tip its landing rebased onto and on the tree it lands, with a nightly whose
`format_version` the tool supports, and ffibox's, with private items, for the contracts of
the forms it defines:

```bash
cargo +<nightly> rustdoc -p <crate> --lib -- -Z unstable-options --output-format json
ffimap api diff <base>.json <tree>.json --dep <ffibox>.json --items "<the worklist's keys>" --format json
```

Each item comes out `kept`, `extended`, `changed`, `removed` or `new`, with its anchor's
move from `Wraps` to `Replaces` where a port made it. The batch's row in the dashboard's
`Batches: API stability` table counts them over its worklist, and over the crate's
unattributed public items, compared per module.

### Accounting › Records

An unseeded scan of the unsafe and FFI surface is recorded at each batch's, wave's and
the campaign's end, as `ffimap.json` in its artifact directory: a batch's in the run dir
of the run that landed it, a wave's in its wave's dir, as `layout` spells it, and the
campaign's in `crustify/artifacts/`. A module's end is the scan of the last wave of its `wrap` and `port` items.

## Reviewing

### Reviewing › Objectives

A review locates the sites of its objectives with a scan, `--sites` with their counters,
and keeps those in its workset: the code its commits add or change, or its modules and
the types, trait impls and functions they name.

- `unsafety`: `fn.unsafe.pub`, `raw_ptr.field.pub`, `raw_ptr.fn_sig_arg.safe.pub` and
  `raw_ptr.fn_sig_ret.safe.pub`.
- `contracts`: `fn.unsafe.pub`, `raw_ptr.fn_sig_arg.unsafe.pub` and
  `raw_ptr.fn_sig_ret.unsafe.pub`, whose `# Safety` obligations are evaluated.
- `ub`: these smells first, in this order:
  1. references into C memory: the references to a cell outside its sanctioned positions,
     `ty.ffibox.wrapper.as.borrowed.std.{pub,priv}` less those shares, and to a raw C
     struct, `ty.ffibox.sys.as.borrowed.std.{pub,priv}`, then
     `raw_ptr.casted_to.std.{borrow,slice,string}`;
  2. thread-safety claims, `ty.impl_trait.of_which.std.send.{pub,priv}` and
     `ty.impl_trait.of_which.std.sync.{pub,priv}`, checked against
     the C library's contract: a data race is reachable from safe code when the library
     does not allow what they assert;
  3. the lifetimes formed inside `unsafe` blocks, found in the source: unsound when the
     handle can outlive the owner of the memory or the point at which C frees or
     invalidates it;
  4. raw pointers a consumer can set, `raw_ptr.fn_sig_arg.safe.pub` and
     `raw_ptr.field.pub`, with their `of_which.void` shares: unsound when a safe path
     dereferences or frees what the consumer passed or stored;
  5. raw-pointer dereferences, `raw_ptr.deref.wr` then `raw_ptr.deref.rd`: first in the
     modules that also hold references into C memory, where a write may invalidate a
     reference, and outside a type's accessors; and
  6. hand-written teardown and copies, `ty.storing_raw_ptr.of_which.impl_drop.{pub,priv}`
     and `ty.storing_raw_ptr.of_which.impl_clone.{pub,priv}`.

## Audit

### Audit workflow › Worksets

The audit's worksets are planned from a scan of the crate, run once each build
configuration it audits is in place, with `--sites` over the counters of its objectives.
A file outside every configuration scanned has no sites, and is planned from its source.

For `ub`, the modules that hold the smells ffimap's review guidance lists for `ub` are
reviewed first, in that order; for `contracts`, those that hold the crate's unsafe API and
its justifications, the `contracts` counters above. The rest of the crate
follows the smells.

The modules are batched by their sites, and a module that is split keeps a type, trait
impl or function with its sites in one batch. A site of `ty.storing_raw_ptr.of_which.impl_drop`,
`.impl_clone`, `ty.impl_trait.of_which.std.send` or `.sync`, at either leaf, is a trait impl, named
`Drop for <type>`, `Clone for <type>`, `Send for <type>` or `Sync for <type>`. Each review
runs the same scan over its own modules, so the sites are not passed on.

---
name: wavefront
description: "Deterministic queries and dependency-ordered plans over the C codebase, the first resort for any question about it: entities, uses, dependencies, pointers, lifecycles, T3 cast tables. Read before querying the C codebase, before planning, decomposing or scheduling, before analysing or binding an item, when packing wrap batches, when reviewing pointer findings or lifecycles, and before changing wavefront itself."
---

# wavefront

Wavefront answers deterministic queries about a C codebase, its entities, their uses and
dependencies, their pointers and lifecycles, and generates dependency-ordered wave plans
over it.

It is the first resort for any question about the C codebase: an entity's definition,
fields or signature, its users, callers and casts, what it depends on, and the pointer
findings and lifecycle roles submitted on it are queried rather than searched for in the
source, so that each answer covers every site the traced build compiles, and every query
of one fact gets one answer. The source is read where wavefront records nothing, to read a
body, and to judge what wavefront records.

Its `README.md` and `--help` are read in full before its first command, and each section
below names the documents under its `docs/` that its stage reads, also in full. How
wavefront scopes, orders and batches, what its configuration, tables and records hold, and
what each query returns are those documents', and are not restated here. Its goals and
non-goals, `docs/goals.md`, are what a change to wavefront is judged against, as
[`evolution`](../../crustify/evolution/SKILL.md) describes.

## Campaign state

Wavefront's repo root is the C root: it is passed `<workdir>/c`, so that every path it
reads and reports is relative to the C root, as the plan records them. Its state sits
under `crustify/wavefront/`, which the configuration names as its `state_dir`,
`../crustify/wavefront`:

- `codeql/`, the CodeQL database and its T1/T2 tables, and `.cache`, both gitignored;
- `configs/wavefront-config.json`, the campaign's configuration, which every query of the
  bindings and reviews resolves through, with `"t3_dir": "t3"`;
- `t3/`, the T3 tables, one campaign-wide pair; and
- `ownership-store.json`, the findings submitted to it through the CLI. A finding
  submitted once is queried again rather than re-derived.

The configuration's `modules` hold one record per module of `modules.json`, named
`<link-unit>/<name>`, with ` (foundational)` after a foundational module's name.

What follows is how wavefront serves each stage: each section names the skill and section
it adds to, and states only what wavefront adds there.

## Batches

### Versioning › Lifecycle › Batches

The CodeQL database and tables under `crustify/wavefront/codeql/`, and wavefront's
`.cache`, are gitignored state every batch needs: they are symlinked into each batch's
worktree once it is forked.

## Binding and porting

Binding and porting read `docs/pointer-properties.md`, `docs/type-lifecycle.md`,
`docs/artifacts/findings.md` and `docs/artifacts/t3.md`.

### Analysis

An item's analysis queries the campaign's configuration, and its findings are submitted
to the ownership store. A type-erased parameter or field is looked up in the T3 tables before it
is bound, and the binding names the type a row gives it rather than a raw pointer. The
instances of a type generator share one generic, with per-instance aliases.

### Binding types › Surface

A type's lifecycle primitives are identified as `docs/type-lifecycle.md` describes, and
submitted to the ownership store.

### Binding symbols › Function pointers

A function pointer's record and its users are those of wavefront's function-pointer query,
named as `docs/graph.md`'s Nodes section names it, and the sites of one written inline,
and what reaches them, are as `docs/batching.md`'s Release points section describes.
<!-- TODO: no query lists an inline function pointer's sites yet: they are read from the
table that section names. -->

### Binding symbols › Lifecycle strategies

Each foundational item's lifecycle role is in the ownership store, where planning
submitted it, and is queried for every item of the batch. A role that the item's body
contradicts is corrected in the ownership store, and the correction named in the batch's commit
message.

### Porting types

A ported type's lifecycle primitives are identified as `docs/type-lifecycle.md`
describes, and submitted to the ownership store.

## Reviewing

### Reviewing › Objectives

#### Lifecycle (`lifecycle`)

Lifecycles submitted to wavefront that are incomplete: a releaser, disposer, cloner or
constructor that the findings of the batches that bound or ported items of the type
route, or items of the foundational modules, missed, checked against the lifecycle
primitives `docs/type-lifecycle.md` identifies.

#### The submitted findings

Whatever the objectives, a review checks the pointer findings an earlier run submitted for
the workset: ownership, access, nullability, cardinality and keepalive. A wrong inference
is a finding.

#### Unsafety

The plan cuts the cycles between modules and types. A raw pointer that stands in for a
dependency a later scheduled batch wraps is such a cut, not an `unsafety` finding.

### Reviewing › Reports

A finding on wavefront's findings is filed in its own `<slug>` directory, with its report
and the evidence that proves the submitted finding wrong or incomplete, under:

- `<reviews dir>/wavefront/ownership/`, for a wrong pointer-related inference; or
- `<reviews dir>/wavefront/lifecycle/`, for an incomplete lifecycle.

A defect in wavefront itself is no finding on its findings: it is a proposal, as any tool
defect is.

### Reviewing › Fixes

Under `fix`, each corrected or completed set of findings is submitted again, and a completed lifecycle gets the representations the Rust is missing.

### Reviewing › Plan corrections

A correction of wavefront's planning artifacts is filed in the reviews sub-directory of
what it amends:

- `crustify/reviews/planner/modules/` for a configuration, with the `modules.json`
  finding it follows from;
- `crustify/reviews/planner/chased-casts/` for `chased_casts.csv`: for each `add` row the
  chain followed, hop by hop with `file:line`, or the hop that breaks it; for each `drop`
  row the cast sites that derive the edge, and why they are no type relation; and
- `crustify/reviews/planner/type-generators/` for `type_generators.csv`: the macro's
  invocation sites, conditional ones included, and the shapes they mint.

A report on a T3 table also states the DAG change the edit makes.

## Evolution

A change to wavefront reads its README's Tests section, which names its opt-in CodeQL
tests: a change to a query or a fixture's C runs them, as the `evolution` skill's Changes
section asks of a tool's opt-in tests.
---
name: ffibox
description: "The library the campaign's Rust holds C memory through, in both directions: owners, handles, lifecycle policies, status conventions, callbacks and exports. Read before writing any wrapper, owner, lifecycle strategy, callable type or export, when judging a crate for adoption, and when testing or reviewing one."
---

# ffibox

ffibox is the library a campaign's Rust expresses C's ownership and lifetime conventions
through, in both directions: memory C allocates, frees, copies, refcounts or locks, held
from Rust behind a safe API, and memory Rust owns that C holds, calls or reads. Its
primitives stand in for raw pointers and hand-written `Drop` impls wherever C aliases a
value; what C does not alias is plain Rust.

Its `README.md` is read in full before the first wrapper is written, and each section
below names the documents under its `docs/` that its stage reads, also in full. Which
primitive serves which C declaration, and how each is built, is those documents'. A
representation ffibox cannot express is hand-written, as its `docs/hand-written.md`
describes, with the same seam and safety-comment discipline. Its goals and non-goals,
`docs/goals.md`, are what a change to ffibox is judged against, as
[`evolution`](../../crustify/evolution/SKILL.md) describes.

What follows is how ffibox serves each stage: each section names the skill and section it
adds to, and states only what ffibox adds there.

## Testing

### Testing › UB tests

The public seam interface ffibox exports on a type is meant to be exercised inside the
crate only, as an escape hatch for external consumers, so it gets no UB tests: a test of
it, for UB or functionality, is a unit test.

## Reviewing

Reviewing reads `docs/goals.md`.

### Reviewing › Objectives

A workset's use of ffibox's primitives is reviewed against ffibox's documentation, and its
hand-written representations against the contract ffibox would have enforced. Under `ub`,
the hazards `docs/goals.md`'s G9 lists are the checklist: each is excluded by the
primitive or the producer's contract it names, or is a finding.

### Reviewing › Reports

A soundness or ergonomics gap in ffibox itself, in its safe primitives or its unsafe FFI
seams, is a defect in a tool: a proposal, as any tool defect is.

Its `README.md` and `--help` are read in full before its first command, and each section
below names the documents under its `docs/` that its stage reads, also in full. How
wavefront scopes, orders and batches, what its configuration, tables and records hold, and
what each query returns are those documents', and are not restated here. Its goals and
non-goals, `docs/goals.md`, are what a change to wavefront is judged against, as
[`evolution`](../../crustify/evolution/SKILL.md) describes.

## Campaign state

Wavefront's repo root is the C root: it is passed `<workdir>/c`, so that every path it
reads and reports is relative to the C root, as the plan records them. Its state sits
under `crustify/wavefront/`, which the configuration names as its `state_dir`,
`../crustify/wavefront`:

- `codeql/`, the CodeQL database and its T1/T2 tables, and `.cache`, both gitignored;
- `configs/wavefront-config.json`, the campaign's configuration, which every query of the
  bindings and reviews resolves through, with `"t3_dir": "t3"`;
- `t3/`, the T3 tables, one campaign-wide pair; and
- `ownership-store.json`, the findings submitted to it through the CLI. A finding
  submitted once is queried again rather than re-derived.

The configuration's `modules` hold one record per module of `modules.json`, named
`<link-unit>/<name>`, with ` (foundational)` after a foundational module's name.

What follows is how wavefront serves each stage: each section names the skill and section
it adds to, and states only what wavefront adds there.

## Batches

### Versioning › Lifecycle › Batches

The CodeQL database and tables under `crustify/wavefront/codeql/`, and wavefront's
`.cache`, are gitignored state every batch needs: they are symlinked into each batch's
worktree once it is forked.

## Binding and porting

Binding and porting read `docs/pointer-properties.md`, `docs/type-lifecycle.md`,
`docs/artifacts/findings.md` and `docs/artifacts/t3.md`.

### Analysis

An item's analysis queries the campaign's configuration, and its findings are submitted
to the ownership store. A type-erased parameter or field is looked up in the T3 tables before it
is bound, and the binding names the type a row gives it rather than a raw pointer. The
instances of a type generator share one generic, with per-instance aliases.

### Binding types › Surface

A type's lifecycle primitives are identified as `docs/type-lifecycle.md` describes, and
submitted to the ownership store.

### Binding symbols › Function pointers

A function pointer's record and its users are those of wavefront's function-pointer query,
named as `docs/graph.md`'s Nodes section names it, and the sites of one written inline,
and what reaches them, are as `docs/batching.md`'s Release points section describes.
<!-- TODO: no query lists an inline function pointer's sites yet: they are read from the
table that section names. -->

### Binding symbols › Lifecycle strategies

Each foundational item's lifecycle role is in the ownership store, where planning
submitted it, and is queried for every item of the batch. A role that the item's body
contradicts is corrected in the ownership store, and the correction named in the batch's commit
message.

### Porting types

A ported type's lifecycle primitives are identified as `docs/type-lifecycle.md`
describes, and submitted to the ownership store.

## Reviewing

### Reviewing › Objectives

#### Lifecycle (`lifecycle`)

Lifecycles submitted to wavefront that are incomplete: a releaser, disposer, cloner or
constructor that the findings of the batches that bound or ported items of the type
route, or items of the foundational modules, missed, checked against the lifecycle
primitives `docs/type-lifecycle.md` identifies.

#### The submitted findings

Whatever the objectives, a review checks the pointer findings an earlier run submitted for
the workset: ownership, access, nullability, cardinality and keepalive. A wrong inference
is a finding.

#### Unsafety

The plan cuts the cycles between modules and types. A raw pointer that stands in for a
dependency a later scheduled batch wraps is such a cut, not an `unsafety` finding.

### Reviewing › Reports

A finding on wavefront's findings is filed in its own `<slug>` directory, with its report
and the evidence that proves the submitted finding wrong or incomplete, under:

- `<reviews dir>/wavefront/ownership/`, for a wrong pointer-related inference; or
- `<reviews dir>/wavefront/lifecycle/`, for an incomplete lifecycle.

A defect in wavefront itself is no finding on its findings: it is a proposal, as any tool
defect is.

### Reviewing › Fixes

Under `fix`, each corrected or completed set of findings is submitted again, and a completed lifecycle gets the representations the Rust is missing.

### Reviewing › Plan corrections

A correction of wavefront's planning artifacts is filed in the reviews sub-directory of
what it amends:

- `crustify/reviews/planner/modules/` for a configuration, with the `modules.json`
  finding it follows from;
- `crustify/reviews/planner/chased-casts/` for `chased_casts.csv`: for each `add` row the
  chain followed, hop by hop with `file:line`, or the hop that breaks it; for each `drop`
  row the cast sites that derive the edge, and why they are no type relation; and
- `crustify/reviews/planner/type-generators/` for `type_generators.csv`: the macro's
  invocation sites, conditional ones included, and the shapes they mint.

A report on a T3 table also states the DAG change the edit makes.

## Evolution

A change to wavefront reads its README's Tests section, which names its opt-in CodeQL
tests: a change to a query or a fixture's C runs them, as the `evolution` skill's Changes
section asks of a tool's opt-in tests.

name: ffibox
description: "The library the campaign's Rust holds C memory through, in both directions: owners, handles, lifecycle policies, status conventions, callbacks and exports. Read before writing any wrapper, owner, lifecycle strategy, callable type or export, when judging a crate for adoption, and when testing or reviewing one."
---

# ffibox

ffibox is the library a campaign's Rust expresses C's ownership and lifetime conventions
through, in both directions: memory C allocates, frees, copies, refcounts or locks, held
from Rust behind a safe API, and memory Rust owns that C holds, calls or reads. Its
primitives stand in for raw pointers and hand-written `Drop` impls wherever C aliases a
value; what C does not alias is plain Rust.

Its `README.md` is read in full before the first wrapper is written, and each section
below names the documents under its `docs/` that its stage reads, also in full. Which
primitive serves which C declaration, and how each is built, is those documents'. A
representation ffibox cannot express is hand-written, as its `docs/hand-written.md`
describes, with the same seam and safety-comment discipline. Its goals and non-goals,
`docs/goals.md`, are what a change to ffibox is judged against, as
[`evolution`](../../crustify/evolution/SKILL.md) describes.

What follows is how ffibox serves each stage: each section names the skill and section it
adds to, and states only what ffibox adds there.

## Testing

### Testing › UB tests

The public seam interface ffibox exports on a type is meant to be exercised inside the
crate only, as an escape hatch for external consumers, so it gets no UB tests: a test of
it, for UB or functionality, is a unit test.

## Reviewing

Reviewing reads `docs/goals.md`.

### Reviewing › Objectives

A workset's use of ffibox's primitives is reviewed against ffibox's documentation, and its
hand-written representations against the contract ffibox would have enforced. Under `ub`,
the hazards `docs/goals.md`'s G9 lists are the checklist: each is excluded by the
primitive or the producer's contract it names, or is a finding.

### Reviewing › Reports

A soundness or ergonomics gap in ffibox itself, in its safe primitives or its unsafe FFI
seams, is a defect in a tool: a proposal, as any tool defect is.
